Now, I know the word itself is provocative. Degrowth. It sounds like decline. It sounds like sacrifice. It sounds like going backward.

But I want to challenge that reaction, because it reveals something important about how deeply growth ideology has colonized our imaginations.

When we hear "less production," we picture empty shelves. When we hear "less consumption," we picture cold homes. That is not what planned degrowth means.

Planned degrowth means asking: What do we actually need to live well? And what are we producing that actively undermines our well-being and our future?

Do we need to produce eighty billion garments a year when a third of them end up in landfills? Do we need planned obsolescence that forces us to replace devices every two years? Do we need SUVs that have grown thirty percent larger while our cities choke on emissions? Do we need a food system that produces enough to feed ten billion people and yet leaves nearly a billion hungry while destroying topsoil and biodiversity?

Degrowth is not about poverty. It is about sufficiency. It is about intentionally scaling down the parts of the economy that are wasteful, destructive, and exploitative—fossil fuels, fast fashion, industrial meat, disposable plastics, speculative finance, planned obsolescence, arms manufacturing—and redirecting our energy, our creativity, and our labor toward what actually sustains life.

It is about more of what matters: more time, more community, more care, more restoration, more democracy, more meaning.

It is about shorter work weeks so parents can be with their children. It is about universal public services—healthcare, housing, education, transport—so that well-being is not held hostage to a paycheck that demands we consume to feel alive. It is about local economies, cooperative ownership, and the radical notion that a good life does not require the relentless accumulation of things.

III. Technology Alone Will Not Save Us

I anticipate the objection. I have heard it a thousand times, and I will hear it a thousand more: "We don't need degrowth. We need green growth. We need innovation. We need decoupling."

I wish that were true. I genuinely wish that were true.

But the empirical record is unforgiving. Absolute decoupling of GDP growth from resource use and carbon emissions at the scale and speed required by climate science has not been achieved by any country on Earth. Not one.

Yes, relative decoupling occurs—we become somewhat more efficient per unit of output. But efficiency gains are consistently overwhelmed by the sheer scale of growth. This is not a new observation. William Stanley Jevons documented it in 1865. We've known about this paradox for over a century and a half, and we are still pretending it doesn't apply to us.

The International Resource Panel tells us that global material extraction has tripled since 1970 and is on pace to double again by 2060. Our ecological footprint continues to expand. Renewables are being added to the energy mix, yes—but global energy consumption keeps rising, and fossil fuel use has not declined in absolute terms.

Technology is essential. Renewable energy is essential. Efficiency is essential. But they are necessary and insufficient. Without addressing the scale of production and consumption, they are merely making the engine of destruction slightly cleaner while pressing the accelerator harder.

You cannot green an economy that is structurally committed to using more every year. At some point, you must ask: how much is enough?

IV. The Courage to Set Limits

And this brings me to what I believe is the deepest challenge—not economic, not technological, but moral and political.

We must find the courage to set limits. Democratically. Justly. Deliberately.

Every sustainable system in nature operates within boundaries. Rivers have banks. Ecosystems have carrying capacities. Seasons have rhythms. The idea that human economies alone are exempt from the logic of limits is not confidence—it is hubris on a civilizational scale.

What would planned degrowth look like in policy? Let me be concrete:

First, we cap resource extraction and carbon emissions with hard, science-based, declining limits—not market-based suggestions, not voluntary pledges, but binding ecological ceilings embedded in law.

Second, we implement a maximum income and wealth cap alongside a robust social floor. No one should live in deprivation, and frankly, no one needs a billion dollars. The concentration of wealth drives overconsumption at the top and desperation at the bottom.

Third, we shorten the working week to thirty hours or fewer, sharing available work more broadly, reducing unemployment, and freeing time for care, community, creativity, and democratic participation.

Fourth, we guarantee universal basic services—public healthcare, education, housing, transport, nutrition, energy—decoupling the necessities of a dignified life from market dependence and the pressure to earn and consume endlessly.

Fifth, we transition and retrain workers in destructive industries with full income protection and public investment in regenerative sectors—ecological restoration, renewable energy, care work, education, sustainable agriculture, and the arts.

Sixth, we redesign our metrics. GDP must be dethroned. We measure what we value, and we have been measuring the wrong things. We need dashboards of well-being, ecological health, equity, health outcomes, democratic participation, and time prosperity.

Seventh, we establish citizens' assemblies on ecological limits, ensuring that these transformations are shaped not by technocrats or corporations, but by ordinary people, informed by the best available science, deliberating about the future they want to live in.

V. Justice Must Be the Foundation

Let me address the concern that weighs most heavily, because it should: justice.

Degrowth without justice would be monstrous. If reducing production simply imposes austerity on those who already have the least, it would be morally indefensible, and I would stand against it alongside you.

That is precisely why degrowth must be planned, democratic, and redistributive. It is not austerity. Austerity cuts public services to protect growth and profit. Degrowth scales down private excess to protect public well-being and the commons.

And let us speak honestly about global justice. The nations most responsible for the ecological crisis—the wealthy, industrialized nations of the Global North—must lead this transition. We cannot ask nations still building basic infrastructure, still lifting people from material deprivation, to bear the cost of a crisis they did not create.

Degrowth is primarily an agenda for the over-consuming nations. It is about the wealthiest societies on Earth finally taking responsibility for their ecological footprint, creating the atmospheric and material space for the Global South to meet the needs of their people within planetary boundaries.

This is not charity. This is debt. Ecological debt. Historical debt. Moral debt. And it is long past due.

VI. What Is Truly Radical?

I will close with this.

I know this vision is called radical. I know it is called unrealistic. I know powerful interests will resist it with every tool at their disposal—because planned degrowth is, at its heart, a threat to the concentration of wealth and power that the growth economy has produced.

But let me ask you: What is truly radical?

Is it radical to suggest that we should live within the means of our planet? Or is it radical to bet the future of every living species on the hope that an economy can grow forever?

Is it radical to propose that people might work less and live more? Or is it radical that we have accepted a system where millions burn out, break down, and die early so that quarterly profits can tick upward?

Is it radical to say that an economy should serve life? Or is it radical that we have built a civilization that treats the living world as raw material and the future as someone else's problem?

The growth economy is the most radical experiment ever conducted on the face of this Earth. It has reshaped the atmosphere, the oceans, the soil, the climate, and the trajectory of evolution itself—all in the span of a few human lifetimes. That is radical. What I am proposing is, in the deepest sense, conservative—it seeks to conserve the conditions for life on this planet.

Friends, we were not put on this Earth to maximize GDP. We are not here to serve an economy. The economy is supposed to serve us—and the living world that sustains us all.

The path of endless growth leads to a place we do not want to go. We know this. In our bones, in our exhaustion, in the anxiety we feel when we look at the world our children will inherit—we know this.

The question is whether we have the courage to choose a different path. Not a path of deprivation, but a path of enough. A path where we measure wealth in clean rivers and living forests and time with the people we love. A path where the economy respects the boundaries of the only home we will ever have.

The technology exists. The policy frameworks exist. The intellectual foundations exist. The movements exist. What we need now is political will—and political will is just another name for collective courage.

So I am asking you—not as an economist, not as a policymaker—but as a human being who shares this fragile, magnificent, irreplaceable planet with eight billion others and countless species beyond our counting:

Let us choose life over growth. Let us choose enough over more. Let us choose a future that our children will not have to survive, but one they will be grateful to inherit.

The age of growth is ending. The question is whether it ends by design or by disaster.

Let us be brave enough to choose design.

Thank you.

What is Planned Economic Degrowth?

Planned economic degrowth refers to a deliberate policy framework aimed at scaling down production, consumption, and overall economic activity in wealthy, industrialized nations (often called the Global North). Unlike traditional economic growth models that prioritize endless expansion of GDP, degrowth seeks a "steady-state" economy that operates within the Earth's finite resource limits. Proponents argue that this is necessary because current growth paradigms are ecologically unsustainable, leading to overexploitation of resources and environmental degradation. The focus is on high-income countries where material wealth has already exceeded basic needs, allowing for intentional downsizing without widespread poverty.

Degrowth policies might include measures like shorter workweeks, reduced advertising, caps on resource extraction, investment in repair and sharing economies, and progressive taxation to discourage overconsumption. The goal is not austerity for its own sake but a managed transition to enhance human well-being while restoring planetary health. Below, I'll outline the supposed benefits and reasons for adopting such policies, with a primary emphasis on addressing environmental limits and promoting ecological sustainability, drawing from ecological economics and environmental science perspectives (e.g., concepts from thinkers like Herman Daly and reports from the IPCC and IPBES).

Reasons to Adopt Degrowth: Addressing Environmental Limits

Modern economies in advanced nations are built on the assumption of infinite growth, but this clashes with the planet's biophysical realities. Earth's systems have clear "limits to growth," as highlighted in the 1972 Limits to Growth report and updated analyses like the 2018 EAT-Lancet planetary boundaries framework. Key reasons for degrowth include:

  1. Overcoming Resource Scarcity and Depletion:

    • Advanced economies consume a disproportionate share of global resources—e.g., the richest 10% of the world's population uses about half of all energy and materials. Continuous growth exacerbates this, leading to depletion of non-renewable resources like fossil fuels, rare earth metals, and freshwater.
    • Degrowth policies aim to reduce throughput (the flow of materials and energy through the economy) by intentionally lowering demand. For instance, by promoting policies like "right to repair" laws or bans on planned obsolescence, societies could extend product lifespans, cutting raw material needs by 20-50% in sectors like electronics and apparel (per Ellen MacArthur Foundation estimates). This addresses limits by aligning consumption with regenerative capacities, preventing scenarios of resource wars or economic collapse.

  2. Mitigating Climate Change and Greenhouse Gas Emissions:

    • The IPCC's reports emphasize that limiting global warming to 1.5°C requires rapid decarbonization, but growth-driven economies in the West account for ~50% of historical emissions despite comprising only ~15% of the global population.
    • By shrinking energy-intensive industries (e.g., via carbon budgets or reduced aviation subsidies), degrowth could slash emissions more effectively than efficiency gains alone, which often lead to "rebound effects" (e.g., fuel-efficient cars enabling more driving). Models from the Degrowth movement suggest that a 50% reduction in energy use in high-income countries could be achieved through voluntary simplicity and relocalization, directly curbing the 70-80 gigatons of CO2-equivalent emissions annually from overconsumption.

  3. Halting Biodiversity Loss and Ecosystem Collapse:

    • Human activities have driven a 68% decline in global wildlife populations since 1970 (WWF Living Planet Report), largely due to habitat destruction for agriculture, mining, and urban expansion fueled by growth imperatives.
    • Degrowth counters this by reducing the "ecological footprint"—a measure showing that advanced economies require 3-5 Earths' worth of resources to sustain current lifestyles. Policies like land-use caps or incentives for rewilding could restore ecosystems, allowing biodiversity to recover. For example, scaling back industrial agriculture (which drives 80% of deforestation) in favor of localized, low-input farming could regenerate soils and forests, enhancing carbon sequestration and resilience to climate shocks.

In essence, degrowth recognizes that environmental limits—such as the nine planetary boundaries (e.g., climate change, biosphere integrity, land-system change)—are being transgressed under growth models. It shifts from "business as usual" to a contraction that buys time for global equity, allowing poorer nations space to develop sustainably without the North monopolizing resources.

Degrowth's proponents claim it fosters long-term ecological health by redesigning economies around sustainability rather than expansion. These benefits are "supposed" in the sense that they rely on equitable implementation; critics argue poor execution could lead to unintended harms, but advocates point to pilot successes like reduced working hours in Denmark or community land trusts in Spain.

  1. Reduced Ecological Footprint and Enhanced Carrying Capacity:

    • By curbing production and consumption, degrowth lowers humanity's overall impact, potentially bringing the global ecological footprint below Earth's biocapacity (currently overshot by ~70%, per Global Footprint Network data). This promotes sustainability by enabling ecosystems to regenerate—e.g., lower fishing quotas could allow marine populations to rebound, sustaining fisheries for future generations.
    • Benefit: A more resilient biosphere, where natural services (e.g., pollination, water purification) are preserved, reducing vulnerability to events like pandemics or floods.

  2. Decoupling Well-Being from Material Throughput:

    • In advanced economies, GDP growth beyond a certain threshold (~$25,000 per capita) yields diminishing returns for happiness and health (Easterlin paradox). Degrowth redirects resources from wasteful consumption (e.g., fast fashion, which generates 10% of global emissions) to ecological restoration, such as massive reforestation or renewable energy transitions without overbuilding.
    • Benefit: Sustainable prosperity, where quality of life improves through non-material means like community gardens or public transport, while ecosystems gain breathing room. Studies from the Netherlands' "circular economy" experiments show that reducing material use by 30% can maintain or boost well-being metrics.

  3. Fostering Systemic Resilience and Adaptation:

    • Growth economies are brittle, prone to crises like the 2008 financial crash or supply chain breakdowns exposed by COVID-19, which strain environments further (e.g., via emergency resource extraction).
    • Degrowth builds resilience by promoting localized, low-energy systems—e.g., community energy cooperatives reduce reliance on global fossil fuel trade, cutting transport emissions by up to 40% (per Transition Towns initiatives). This sustains ecosystems by minimizing disruptions, like oil spills or habitat fragmentation from mega-infrastructure.
    • Benefit: A "safe operating space" for humanity (Rockström et al., 2009), where ecological tipping points (e.g., Amazon dieback) are avoided, ensuring long-term habitability.

Challenges and Broader Context

While degrowth offers a radical response to environmental limits, it's not without critique: implementation requires global cooperation to avoid "carbon leakage" (emissions shifting to unregulated areas), and it must prioritize justice to prevent disproportionate burdens on marginalized groups. Title: Embracing Planned Economic Degrowth: A Moral Imperative for Ecological Survival

Introduction
Humanity stands at a precipice. The relentless pursuit of economic growth in advanced industrial economies has unleashed an unprecedented ecological crisis, threatening the very foundations of life. The Earth’s ecosystems are under siege. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) warns that global temperatures could rise by 3°C by 2100, triggering irreversible tipping points such as the collapse of ice sheets and the die-off of coral reefs. Biodiversity loss is equally alarming: the planet has lost 83% of wild mammals and 45% of marine species since the industrial era began. The Jennie S. These crises stem from economies that operate within planetary boundaries defined by Kevin Anderson and Peter Glikson, yet exceed them by exploiting finite resources at unsustainable rates.

The concept of the "doughnut model" by Kate Raworth illustrates this imbalance: humanity has burst through the outer boundary of ecological overshoot while leaving billions in poverty inside the inner ring of social deprivation. Growth-oriented economies, measured by Gross Domestic Product (GDP), conflate material throughput with progress. However, GDP ignores environmental degradation and social inequality. As economist Herman Daly quipped, “GDP is a measure of the speed of the canoe, not the size of the hole in the bottom.” Without radical change, ecological collapse is inevitable.

Proponents of "green growth" argue that technological innovation and efficiency can decouple economic growth from environmental harm. Yet this remains a theoretical fantasy. A 2021 study in Nature Ecology & Evolution found that relative decoupling (reducing environmental impact per unit of GDP) is common, but absolute decoupling (reducing total environmental impact despite growth) is rare and insufficient. For instance, while renewable energy adoption grows, so does global energy consumption, negating gains. This is compounded by the "rebound effect," where efficiency improvements (e.g., LED lighting) lower costs and spur increased demand, offsetting savings.

Moreover, growth-driven systems inherently prioritize extraction. The World Bank estimates that raw material use in OECD countries will increase by 50% by 2060 if current trends continue. Green growth also relies on unproven technologies like carbon capture and storage (CCS), which risk becoming "permits to pollute." As climate activist Greta Thunberg asserts, "We are still in the beginning of the climate crisis, and we are failing." To rely on growth-compatible solutions is to gamble with the planet’s future.

Degrowth, far from advocating for economic collapse, envisions a managed transition to localized, equitable, and sustainable economies. Degrowth also demands rethinking global equity. Advanced economies must support developing nations’ sustainable development, recognizing historical responsibility. As scholar Jason Hickel emphasizes, degrowth is not about making poor countries poorer but about rich countries consuming less to allow others to thrive.

Conclusion
Planned economic degrowth is the ethical imperative of our time. It challenges the dogma of growth, which has brought us to the brink of ecological ruin. By reducing material throughput, prioritizing equity, and redefining prosperity, degrowth offers a path to both ecological survival and human flourishing. The choice is clear: continue down a trajectory of collapse or embrace a future where economies serve life, not the other way around. Degrowth addresses this by advocating for a planned contraction: reducing energy-intensive production, curbing unnecessary consumption through policies like resource caps and consumption taxes, and redirecting resources toward regenerative activities. Far from being a fringe idea, this is a survival strategy. Without it, we risk tipping points like Amazon dieback or permafrost thaw, rendering vast regions uninhabitable. Introduction

For decades, advanced industrial economies have pursued relentless economic growth as the primary measure of progress and well-being. The fundamental issue with perpetual economic growth is that it requires ever-increasing extraction of resources, energy, and labor, all of which strain ecosystem resilience. The global ecological footprint far exceeds Earth’s biocapacity, meaning humanity is already extracting more than the planet can regenerate. Key environmental crises include:

  3. Resource Depletion – From rare earth minerals to water, the global economy is rapidly depleting non-renewable resources. A degrowth model would prioritize sufficiency over excess, reducing waste and extending the lifespan of finite reserves.

Continued growth under these conditions is ecological suicide. Degrowth, by contrast, aligns economic systems with planetary boundaries, ensuring long-term sustainability.

The Case Against Growth-Based Capitalism

Advocates of economic growth argue that mankindustrates constant expansion as necessary for prosperity, yet empirical evidence suggests otherwise:

  1. The Jevons Paradox – Greater efficiency in resource use often increases total consumption rather than decreasing it (e.g., more fuel-efficient cars leading to more driving). Degrowth disrupts this feedback loop by limiting overall demand.

  3. The Limits to Growth – The 1972 Limits to Growth study (and subsequent updates) confirmed that unchecked growth leads to environmental and economic collapse. Only by reducing GDP through deliberate policy can society avoid catastrophic tipping points.

The alternative—endless growth—will inevitably lead to societal breakdown when ecosystems collapse. Degrowth is not austerity; it is a planned, just transition to a sustainable and equitable economy.

How Degrowth Can Be Implemented Fairly

Critics of degrowth fear lowered standards of living, but historical precedent shows that post-growth economies can enhance well-being:

  1. Redefining Prosperity – GDP is a flawed metric that ignores social and ecological well-being. Degrowth prioritizes indicators like human happiness, health, and ecological health, as seen in the success of the Gross National Happiness index in Bhutan.

  3. Localized and Low-Tech Economies – Degrowth favors decentralized, circular economies that minimize waste and pollution. This includes regenerative agriculture, reduced industrial output, and strengthened local supply chains.

Conclusion

The pursuit of endless economic growth is a dangerous delusion that threatens civilizational survival. Ecological breakdown is not a distant possibility but an accelerating reality. Planned degrowth is the only viable path to stabilize the climate, restore biodiversity, and create a just society. Far from being a rejection of progress, degrowth represents a fundamental reorientation toward sustainability, equity, and long-term flourishing. The choice is clear: continue down the path of ecological ruin, or embrace degrowth as a deliberate and necessary policy for our collective future. The stakes could not be higher.

  • Growth-centric capitalism exacerbates inequality, as benefits often accrue to the wealthy while costs are externalized to marginalized communities and future generations.
  • Degrowth shifts focus to redistribution, universal basic services (UBI), and cooperatives, ensuring basic needs are met without endless expansion.

5. Building Resilient Local Economies

  • Globalized, high-consumption economies are vulnerable to supply chain disruptions, resource scarcity, and financial crises.
  • Degrowth encourages localized production, circular economies, and regeneration, enhancing food and energy security.
  • Policies like public ownership of key resources (e.g., water, energy) prevent privatization-driven exploitation.

  • GDP growth does not correspond to human well-being beyond a certain point (the "happiness threshold").

  • Modern economies are plagued by planned obsolescence, excess packaging, and food waste.
  • Degrowth encourages durable goods, repair cultures, and closed-loop systems, minimizing waste streams.

Potential Challenges & Criticisms

  • Feasibility: Transitioning from growth-based systems requires strong political and social will.
  • Global Inequalities: Rich nations reducing consumption alone will not solve systemic problems without global redistributive policies.
  • Technological vs. Degrowth Solutions: Some argue efficiency and innovation (e.g., green tech) can decouple growth from harm, but degrowth advocates argue this is insufficient.

Conclusion

Degrowth is not about poverty but about sharing resources more fairly, working less, and living lighter on the planet.
